title: Who Benefits from Education Savings Accounts? Q&A with Susha Roy
gist: RAND's Susha Roy, studying Arizona's pioneering K-12 education savings account program, finds ESA users skewed toward wealthier neighborhoods and higher-achieving districts, many were already in private school, and private school tuition rose after the accounts became available - evidence of cream skimming and possible price capture rather than expanded access. She argues outcomes are unmeasurable today and calls for persistent student IDs across sectors to track them.

insights.claim: Education savings accounts redirect the per-student state funding that would have gone to a public school directly to the family, spendable on private school tuition, tutoring, homeschooling expenses or textbooks.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Defines the money flow: ESAs convert institutional school budgets into household purchasing power, creating a direct consumer market for education services.
insights.quote: They essentially take the money that would have been allocated for a student in public school and make it available directly to the family.

insights.claim: ESAs originated mainly as a mechanism for students with disabilities to access specialized services, but a growing number of states have now opened them to all families - a shift from targeted to universal eligibility.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Universal eligibility is what turns a niche program into a large, addressable market and changes who captures the subsidy.
insights.locator: Such accounts have been around for years

insights.claim: Federal tax credits taking effect this year let families write off up to $1,700 in contributions to scholarship-granting organizations for similar education services and expenses.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: A new federal subsidy layer stacked on state ESAs expands demand for private education providers beyond the ESA states themselves.
insights.quote: Federal tax credits kicking in this year will also allow families to write off up to $1,700
insights.locator: Tens of thousands of American families

themes.theme: Who actually benefits - cream skimming evidence

insights.claim: The two groups that have genuinely benefited from ESAs are students trapped in underperforming neighborhood schools and students with specialized disabilities whose needs public schools cannot individually meet.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: The defensible policy case for ESAs is narrow and targeted, which is the argument that survives scrutiny when universal programs come under attack.
insights.locator: There are two main categories of students

insights.claim: A large number of students with autism use education savings accounts in Arizona, because the support they need is too varied for public schools to reliably provide.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Identifies a concentrated, funded demand pocket for specialized autism therapy and education providers.
insights.locator: The other category is students with disabilities

insights.claim: In Arizona, ESA users tended to live in wealthier neighborhoods and came from higher-achieving public school districts, a clear cream-skimming pattern in which participants are not the students the program could help most.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: The flagship ESA state shows the subsidy flowing upward, which is the core empirical ammunition for opponents and for redesign mandates.
insights.quote: We found a pretty clear pattern of this in Arizona
insights.locator: There have also been concerns about

insights.claim: Because families will not automatically know how to use new accounts, states that want broad access must actively prioritize outreach to the families who could benefit most rather than assuming uptake will self-distribute.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Program design and outreach spend, not eligibility rules alone, determine distributional outcomes - a lever states will be pushed to pull.
insights.quote: If states want to expand access to educational opportunities for all students, they could consider prioritizing outreach to families who could benefit the most.
insights.locator: Now, early adopters of any education program

insights.claim: Because most states tie public school funding to enrollment, students leaving for ESAs cut a school's state revenue while fixed costs such as building maintenance persist, creating a structural squeeze even if staffing shrinks.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Enrollment-linked funding plus sticky fixed costs is the mechanism behind district budget stress, closures and municipal credit pressure in high-ESA states.
insights.locator: Most states tie state funding for public schools to student enrollment

insights.claim: Many Arizona students receiving education savings accounts were already enrolled in private school, meaning the state was substituting public money for existing private spending rather than moving students out of public schools.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Deadweight subsidy: fiscal cost rises without a matching enrollment shift, the strongest budget-side critique of universal ESAs.
insights.locator: What we saw in Arizona, though

insights.claim: Private school tuition rose when education savings accounts became available in Arizona, with the possible mechanism being that schools raised prices to capture the additional state funding flowing to families.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Subsidy capture by providers - the classic voucher-inflation dynamic - means ESA dollars may accrue to private school pricing power rather than to families.
insights.quote: it could be that schools raised their tuition to try to capture the additional state funding that families had coming in
insights.locator: And we found evidence that private school tuition went up

insights.claim: Without accountability mechanisms, ESA programs risk simply inflating the cost of private school and subsidizing families already using it, with no assurance that school quality improves.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Frames the regulatory tail risk: expect accountability strings to be attached as programs mature and costs surprise to the upside.
insights.quote: you might just inflate the cost of private school and subsidize families whose kids were already going to private school anyway
insights.locator: It goes back to how you design these programs

themes.theme: Measurement gap and the policy fix

insights.claim: States currently cannot determine whether ESA spending benefits children because outcome data on how account-holding students perform in receiving schools is not collected.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: The evidence vacuum is why the debate stays ideological - the first credible outcome study becomes a major policy catalyst.
insights.quote: Without that, we just won't know for sure whether the money states spend on education savings accounts benefits children.
insights.locator: If you were advising state leaders

insights.claim: Some states are exploring a persistent student ID that follows a child across education sectors, which would for the first time allow tracking of student outcomes between public and private settings.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: A cross-sector student identifier is the enabling infrastructure for ESA accountability - watch which states adopt it as a leading indicator of tighter rules.
insights.quote: A few have talked about having a student ID that stays with students as they move between sectors.

insights.claim: What ESAs will mean for students, academic achievement and the future of public schools remains far from clear even as tens of thousands of families now hold them.
insights.speaker: Susha Roy
insights.so_what: Policy is running well ahead of evidence, which raises the odds of abrupt reversals or retrofits in fast-expanding states.
insights.locator: What all this will mean for students
